direction_as_read: Small positive trials at label-range amounts on self-reported respiratory symptoms, a positive adult meta-analysis at 10 g to 20 g daily, and null or mixed laboratory immune markers at higher doses
summary: The labels print bovine colostrum or colostrum at 400 mg to 900 mg, and a 1 g proprietary concentrate, mostly with an immune purpose. One trial meets the rule: 500 mg to 1 g daily in healthy pre-school children, with symptom frequency and gravity named as primary outcomes in the full text and both favouring colostrum (37630816). It was small, used self-report, had uneven exclusions and had a manufacturer tie. The adult meta-analysis is positive but used 10 g or 20 g daily, and its own trials did not make symptoms primary (27462401).
question_for_clinician: 37630816 meets rule 2 on its face for 500 mg bovine colostrum: RCT, colostrum alone with a banana carrier, primary outcomes named in the full text, both positive. Should any of the 8 labels get credit on this? Agent recommendation: no credit, direction stays positive_weak. The one rule 2 trial is 57 pre-school children with self-reported symptoms, a post-randomization response filter and a manufacturer tie, and adult evidence at label amounts (37111143) names no primary outcome.

outcomes.name: Frequency of days with any URTI symptoms: 31% median reduction versus placebo, significant until week 20
Average gravity score of URTI symptoms: 37% median reduction versus placebo

limitations: Children only; these labels print no age group and carry a general immune purpose.
Symptoms were reported by online survey and not confirmed by testing.

Before the start, 14 participants were excluded for not collecting product (2 colostrum, 12 placebo), and 13 more were excluded from analysis for poor survey response (5 colostrum, 8 placebo), so the analysis isn't full intention to treat and group sizes are uneven.
Material was freeze-dried colostrum collected within 2 hours of calving, mixed 1 to 1 with banana powder; no label prints the collection time.
The manufacturer supplied the product free of charge, and one author is paid by the manufacturer.

read_not_used.35745242: Systematic review of nine gut permeability studies in athletes; the abstract calls for well-designed trials and gives no pooled effect.
read_not_used.29274034: 20 g/day in 31 men: no difference in summed skin response, greater sensitivity at low antigen doses. Far above label amounts; laboratory immune model.
read_not_used.42249952: Acute 30 g plus 5 g plus 5 g around cycling, 16 men: mixed laboratory immune markers. Far above label amounts.
read_not_used.39497827: 25 g/day for 12 weeks, 28 athletes: higher post-exercise salivary SIgA, no effect on blood immunoglobulins. Far above label amounts; no clinical outcome.
read_not_used.38004173: 24 week crossover in 28 football players: higher IgG and lower inflammatory markers, no effect on performance; the abstract states no dose and no primary outcome.
read_not_used.33396972: 3.2 g twice daily for 24 weeks in 20 young female basketball players: no significant effects on immune indicators apart from an IL-10 change in both groups.
read_not_used.25727914: 20 g/day for 4 weeks, 20 participants: greater fMLP-stimulated oxidative burst, no effect on other immune markers. Far above label amounts.
read_not_used.33077128: 14 days in 10 males: no effect on salivary lactoferrin or lysozyme; the abstract states no dose.
read_not_used.28290057: 20 g/day crossover, 18 males: lower post-exercise permeability, used as a positive control. Far above label amounts.
read_not_used.30551120: Early enteral colostrum in ICU patients: lower endotoxin, zonulin and diarrhea; enteral critical care setting, no dose in the abstract.
read_not_used.42626164: Children with kidney anomalies and recurrent UTIs: overall reduction not significant, RR 0.84, p = 0.22; a purpose these labels do not carry.
